```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
has_lme4    <- requireNamespace("lme4", quietly = TRUE)
has_ggplot2 <- requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)
```

Manual review is the most expensive step of the workflow, so the number of
clips to validate per site x species is a design decision. sheepdog offers
two complementary views of it:

* **Stage 2, `calibration_effort()`.** The cross-validated AUC of a
  calibration model as a function of the number of reviewed clips per
  site x species cell. It answers whether, pooled over all cells, more clips
  would still improve the calibration.
* **Stage 1, `precision_by_bin()` and `suggest_thresholds()`.** Precision
  by confidence bin and the lowest threshold that reaches a target
  precision, for each site x species, with flags for bins and thresholds
  resting on few clips. They show *which* cells lack support, and, with
  `covariate_bins()`, which parts of an environmental gradient or of the
  acoustic background.

This vignette runs both on the simulated example shipped with the package.

## Example data

The example holds BirdNET predictions simulated for frog species at
several sites over six months (`data-raw/make_example_data.R` in the source
repository). False-positive confidences overlap those of true detections,
and false-positive rates differ among species and sites. The reviewed clips
were drawn with the `"top"` design (the two highest confidences per
site x species x night x hour, up to 80 clips per site x species) and their
verdicts come from the simulated truth. Species with few detections at a
site yield fewer than 80 clips there.

```{r}
library(sheepdog)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

ex <- system.file("extdata", "example", package = "sheepdog")
val_files <- list.files(file.path(ex, "validation"), full.names = TRUE)
basename(val_files)
```

`read_validations()` stacks the tables and keeps the clips with a verdict
and a confidence score, in the form used by the calibration models:

```{r}
val <- read_validations(val_files)
val |>
  summarise(precision = round(mean(tp), 2), .by = c(site, species)) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = species, values_from = precision)
```

The table gives the share of true positives among the reviewed clips of
each cell (`r n_distinct(val$species)` species x `r n_distinct(val$site)`
sites = `r n_distinct(paste(val$site, val$species))` cells of
`r paste(unique(range(count(val, site, species)$n)), collapse = " to ")`
clips). It already shows that the same design yields very different
precision across species and sites.

## Stage 2: the effort curve

### How the curve is built

For each training size *n* in `n_train`, `calibration_effort()` draws *n*
clips from every site x species cell (keeping at least five per cell for
testing), fits the model to the drawn clips and computes the AUC on all the
remaining clips. This is repeated `n_reps` times per *n*; repetitions whose
fit fails, or with fewer than 50 test clips, are dropped. The result gives,
for each *n*, the mean and standard deviation of the AUC across
repetitions.

The candidate formulas come from `calibration_models()`, and
`compare_calibration_models()` ranks them by 5-fold cross-validation on all
the clips (formulas with random effects need the 'lme4' package):

```{r, eval = has_lme4}
models <- calibration_models()
cv <- compare_calibration_models(val, models)
select(cv, model, auc_mean, auc_sd)
```

```{r, eval = !has_lme4, include = FALSE}
models <- calibration_models()
```

The effort curve below is drawn for the global model (`m0_global`, a
single logistic regression on the logit of the score) and for the
hierarchical `m4_species_x_site` (random slopes by species and a
site x species intercept), the structure used by FrogNet.

The vignette uses few repetitions so that it renders quickly. In real use
keep the default of 50 repetitions (or more): the standard deviation is
itself estimated from `n_reps` values and is unstable with few
repetitions. Training sizes must stay below the size of the smallest cell
minus five, since at most `n - 5` clips of a cell are used for training
whatever the value of `n_train`. `calibration_effort()` warns when a
requested size exceeds that limit, and reports the training size actually
used (`n_train_mean`), the size of the test set (`n_test_mean`) and the
repetitions dropped (`n_failed`) next to the AUC.

```{r}
cell_min <- min(count(val, site, species)$n)
cell_min
n_train <- c(5, 10, 15, 20, 25)
n_reps  <- 15
```

The smallest cell holds `r cell_min` clips, so the largest training size
that every cell can supply is `r cell_min - 5`, and `n_train` stops below
it. Larger sizes would trigger the warning, and `n_train_mean` would fall
below `n_per_cell`: the small cells would contribute fewer clips than
requested, and the curve would no longer describe a uniform effort per
cell. To explore larger efforts, draw the curve on the subset of cells
large enough to supply them, keeping in mind that this subset excludes
the species with few detections, often the hardest to calibrate.

### The two curves

```{r}
eff_m0 <- calibration_effort(val, models$m0_global,
                             n_train = n_train, n_reps = n_reps)
eff_m0
```

```{r, eval = has_lme4}
eff_m4 <- calibration_effort(val, models$m4_species_x_site,
                             n_train = n_train, n_reps = n_reps)
eff_m4
```

The draws depend only on `seed`, `n_train`, `n_reps` and the data, not on
the formula, so with the same arguments both curves are computed on the
same training and test sets and can be compared repetition by repetition.

```{r, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4, fig.alt = "Mean cross-validated AUC, with plus or minus one standard deviation, against the number of reviewed clips per site x species cell, for the global and the hierarchical calibration models.", eval = has_ggplot2}
effort <- bind_rows(m0_global = eff_m0,
                    m4_species_x_site = if (has_lme4) eff_m4,
                    .id = "model")

library(ggplot2)
ggplot(effort, aes(n_per_cell, auc_mean, colour = model)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = auc_mean - auc_sd, ymax = auc_mean + auc_sd),
                  position = position_dodge(width = 2)) +
  labs(x = "Reviewed clips per site x species (training)",
       y = "Cross-validated AUC (mean ± sd)", colour = "Model") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r, include = FALSE}
# smallest n whose mean AUC is within `tol` of the best mean of the curve
plateau <- function(eff, tol = 0.005) {
  with(eff, min(n_per_cell[auc_mean >= max(auc_mean) - tol]))
}
auc_at <- function(eff, n) round(eff$auc_mean[eff$n_per_cell == n], 3)
n_lo  <- min(n_train)
n_mid <- 20
n_hi  <- max(n_train)
# test clips left with the largest training size
n_test_max <- round(eff_m0$n_test_mean[eff_m0$n_per_cell == n_hi])
```

### Reading the curve

**Which formula.** The curve belongs to a model, not to the data. The
mean AUC of the global model stays between
`r round(min(eff_m0$auc_mean), 3)` and `r round(max(eff_m0$auc_mean), 3)`
at every training size: it has only two parameters, which are estimated
well from a few clips per cell, and more clips cannot correct its
structural limitation, that one score-to-probability curve is shared by
all species and sites.
`r if (has_lme4) paste0("The hierarchical model is higher at every size (", auc_at(eff_m4, n_lo), " with ", n_lo, " clips per cell, ", auc_at(eff_m4, n_mid), " with ", n_mid, " and ", auc_at(eff_m4, n_hi), " with ", n_hi, ") and, unlike the global model, it gains from additional clips, because each clip also informs the species- and site-specific terms.") else "With 'lme4' installed, this vignette also draws the curve of the hierarchical model."`
The gap between the curves is the gain from modelling how species and
sites differ; its size, not only the height of either curve, is what the
choice of formula rests on. Draw the curve for the formula that
`compare_calibration_models()` selects (or that `calibrate()` refits), with
`m0_global` as a baseline.

**Where it flattens.** Beyond the training size at which the mean AUC stops
increasing, extra clips in every cell add little discrimination. With a
tolerance of 0.005 below the best mean AUC of each curve (an illustrative
choice, not a rule of the package), the global model is flat from
`r plateau(eff_m0)` clips per cell`r if (has_lme4) paste0(" and the hierarchical model from ", plateau(eff_m4))`.
`r if (has_lme4) paste0("For the hierarchical model the gain per clip falls with effort: the first ", 10 - n_lo, " extra clips per cell (from ", n_lo, " to 10) add ", round(auc_at(eff_m4, 10) - auc_at(eff_m4, n_lo), 3), " to the mean AUC, and the next ", n_hi - 10, " (from 10 to ", n_hi, ") add ", round(auc_at(eff_m4, n_hi) - auc_at(eff_m4, 10), 3), " in total.")`
The first clips of a cell fix its intercept and slope; the later ones only
refine them. Whether the curve keeps rising beyond `r cell_min - 5` clips
per cell cannot be assessed with every cell in the curve (see above). Small dips in the mean between neighbouring training sizes
are within the spread of the repetitions and should not be read as losses.

**The variability across repetitions.** At small *n* the standard
deviation measures how much the calibration depends on *which* clips were
reviewed; a large spread means that a single validation round of that size
may produce a poor model by chance.
`r if (has_lme4) paste0("For the hierarchical model it is largest with ", n_lo, " clips per cell (sd = ", round(eff_m4$auc_sd[1], 3), ") and halves by ", eff_m4$n_per_cell[which(eff_m4$auc_sd <= eff_m4$auc_sd[1] / 2)[1]], ".")`
The spread can also grow with *n* for a different reason: the test set is
what is left of each cell, so it shrinks as *n* grows (`n_test_mean`; with
`r n_hi` training clips per cell, `r n_test_max` of the `r nrow(val)` clips
remain for testing). The standard deviation of the global model, which
gains nothing from extra clips, rises from `r round(eff_m0$auc_sd[1], 3)`
to `r round(eff_m0$auc_sd[nrow(eff_m0)], 3)` for that reason alone.

AUC measures discrimination (whether true detections score higher than
false ones), not whether the calibrated probabilities are accurate. A curve
that has flattened does not imply that the species- or site-specific curves
of `plot_calibration()` are well estimated in every cell; that is what the
per-cell view of stage 1 checks.

## Stage 1: which cells lack support

The effort curve pools all cells. `precision_by_bin()` and
`suggest_thresholds()` work cell by cell on the `validation_by_clip.csv`
tables (the output of `post_validation()`), so they read the raw tables
rather than the output of `read_validations()`:

```{r}
val_raw <- purrr::map(val_files, readr::read_csv, show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  purrr::list_rbind()

prec <- precision_by_bin(val_raw, min_n = 15)
prec |>
  filter(site == "BAI", species_folder %in% c("phy_cuv", "pse_pla")) |>
  mutate(precision = round(precision, 2)) |>
  select(species_folder, bin, n = n_reviewed, precision) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = species_folder,
                     values_from = c(n, precision)) |>
  arrange(bin)
```

A bin is flagged `low_support` when it holds fewer than `min_n` reviewed
clips (here, bins with `n` below 15). The two cells shown differ in how
the flags should be read. For *phy_cuv* at BAI the reviewed clips
concentrate in the upper bins, as expected from the `"top"` design, and
precision there is high; the flagged low bins matter only if the study
needs a low threshold. For *pse_pla* at BAI the clips spread over the
whole range and precision stays low at high scores, including the upper bins
that reach `min_n`:
the classifier confuses this species at high scores, and more clips would
not change that.

`suggest_thresholds()` returns, for each cell, the lowest confidence at
which precision reaches `target_precision` with at least `min_n` clips
above it (`NA` when no cut does):

```{r}
thr <- suggest_thresholds(val_raw, target_precision = 0.90, min_n = 15)
thr |>
  mutate(threshold = if_else(is.na(threshold), "-",
                             format(threshold, nsmall = 2))) |>
  select(site, species_folder, threshold) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = species_folder, values_from = threshold)
```

The target is reached in `r sum(!is.na(thr$threshold))` of the
`r nrow(thr)` cells. A missing threshold has two possible causes, and they
call for opposite decisions: too few reviewed clips at high scores (more
review may help) or low precision even at high scores (more review will
not). To tell them apart, count the high-score clips reviewed in each cell,
their precision, and how many high-score detections in the complete
selection tables were not reviewed:

```{r}
conf_high <- 0.7   # example: what counts as a high score
min_n     <- 15

detections <- suppressMessages(
  read_selection_tables(file.path(ex, "birdnet"))) |>
  mutate(species = gsub("-", "_", sub("^.*_", "", species_code)))

support <- val |>
  mutate(across(c(site, species), as.character)) |>
  summarise(n_fp      = sum(tp == 0),
            n_high    = sum(confidence >= conf_high),
            prec_high = round(mean(tp[confidence >= conf_high]), 2),
            .by = c(site, species)) |>
  left_join(detections |>
              summarise(n_high_all = sum(confidence >= conf_high),
                        .by = c(site, species)),
            by = c("site", "species")) |>
  left_join(select(thr, site, species = species_folder, threshold),
            by = c("site", "species")) |>
  mutate(unreviewed_high = n_high_all - n_high,
         diagnosis = case_when(
           !is.na(threshold)        ~ "reached",
           unreviewed_high < min_n  ~ "exhausted",
           prec_high < 0.5          ~ "unreliable",
           .default = "review more"
         )) |>
  select(site, species, n_fp, n_high, prec_high, unreviewed_high,
         diagnosis) |>
  arrange(diagnosis, species, site)
print(support, n = Inf)
```

```{r, include = FALSE}
cells_with <- function(d) {
  x <- filter(support, diagnosis == d)
  if (nrow(x) == 0) return("none")
  paste(x$species, x$site, sep = " at ", collapse = ", ")
}
```

A cell is `"reached"` when `suggest_thresholds()` found a threshold. The
other labels use illustrative cut-offs (`conf_high`, `min_n` and a
precision of 0.5 at high scores); set them from the precision the study
needs. In this example they separate three groups of cells that lack
support:

* **`"review more"`:** `r cells_with("review more")`.
  Precision at high scores is intermediate and unreviewed high-score
  detections remain, so a further round of review restricted to high
  scores in these cells may reveal a cut that reaches the target.
* **`"exhausted"`:** `r cells_with("exhausted")`.
  The `"top"` design has already taken almost every high-score detection
  of these cells; more effort cannot add support. Treat the species at that
  site as poorly calibrated. In this example these cells have
  `r sum(filter(count(val, site, species, wt = tp), paste(species, site) %in% with(filter(support, diagnosis == "exhausted"), paste(species, site)))$n)`
  true positives among their reviewed clips in total (see `n_fp` below).
* **`"unreliable"`:** `r cells_with("unreliable")`.
  Most high-score detections are false positives; more review would only
  confirm it. These cells call for retraining the classifier (with the
  clips of `retraining_clips()`) rather than for more validation.

The column `n_fp` deserves a look of its own. The calibration slope is
estimated from the contrast between true and false positives, so a cell
with few false positives (here as few as `r min(support$n_fp)`) carries
little information about the low end of its calibration curve, even when
its total number of reviewed clips is large. At the other extreme,
a cell whose reviewed clips are all false positives
(`r with(filter(count(val, site, species, wt = tp), n == 0), if (length(species) > 0) paste(species, site, sep = " at ", collapse = ", ") else "none in this example")`)
gives no information on true detections at all; it may be a site where the
species is absent. These are interpretations of the model structure, not
flags computed by the package.

## Stage 1 along a gradient

The checks above split the reviewed clips by site x species. The share of
false positives can also change along an environmental gradient within a
site, for instance with the temperature or the rain of the night, or with
the acoustic background of the recording (wind, rain, a chorus of other
species). When the gradient is also a covariate of occupancy, a model with
false positives can only separate the two effects if the reviewed clips
cover the whole gradient, including its ends, which hold few nights and
are easily missed by a draw that ignores them. Two steps make the gradient
part of the design: stratify the draw of `select_clips()` by bins of the
covariate, and repeat the checks of stage 1 within each bin.

### Bins of the covariate

`covariate_bins()` cuts a covariate of the occasions into bins. The table
should list every night (or recording) of the study, with or without
predictions, so that the same bins serve the draw and every later table.
The covariates of the example are **simulated** here, independently of the
verdicts, only to show the mechanics: a mean temperature per night and an
acoustic index per recording.

```{r}
recordings <- read.csv(file.path(ex, "recordings.csv")) |>
  mutate(occasion_id = tools::file_path_sans_ext(
           basename(gsub("\\\\", "/", source_audio))),
         night = sub("^.*_(\\d{8})_\\d{6}$", "\\1", occasion_id))

set.seed(42)
nights <- distinct(recordings, site, night) |>
  mutate(temp = rnorm(n(), mean = 22, sd = 3))
temp_bins <- covariate_bins(nights, "temp", key = c("site", "night"),
                            n_bins = 3)
count(temp_bins, site, temp_bin) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = temp_bin, values_from = n)
```

By default the breaks are the quantiles of the covariate **within each
site** (`within = "site"`), so each site contributes nights to every bin.
Quantiles over all sites (`within = NULL`) or fixed breaks (`breaks = `)
suit a covariate measured on the same scale everywhere, such as rainfall;
an acoustic index depends on the gain and placement of each recorder, so
its bins should be computed within sites.

### Drawing clips along the gradient

The bin enters `strata`, and the table of bins enters `covariates`; it is
joined to the predictions by the columns they share (here `site` and
`night`). Every site x species x bin stratum then gets `n_top` occasions:

```{r}
detections_raw <- suppressMessages(
  read_selection_tables(file.path(ex, "birdnet")))
clips_temp <- select_clips(detections_raw, "random_detections",
                           threshold = 0.5, n_top = 3, strata = "temp_bin",
                           covariates = temp_bins)
clips_temp |>
  distinct(site, species_code, occasion_id, night) |>
  left_join(temp_bins, by = c("site", "night")) |>
  count(temp_bin)
```

The bin does not depend on the score, so `inclusion_prob` stays exact.
The message printed by `select_clips()` is a reminder of the main caveat,
discussed below. The clip manifest keeps its usual columns; the bin comes
back from the same `temp_bins` table whenever it is needed.

An acoustic index works the same way, with the recording as key. With
`occasion_unit = "minute"`, the key would be `occasion_id` of each minute:

```{r}
aci <- recordings |>
  mutate(aci = rnorm(n(), mean = 150, sd = 10)) |>
  select(site, occasion_id, aci)
aci_bins <- covariate_bins(aci, "aci", key = c("site", "occasion_id"),
                           n_bins = 2)
clips_aci <- select_clips(detections_raw, "random_detections",
                          threshold = 0.5, n_top = 3,
                          strata = c("month", "aci_bin"),
                          covariates = aci_bins)
```

Here the strata cross the index with the month, so that quiet and noisy
recordings are reviewed in every month; in a real study this would let
the checks tell a change in calling activity from a change in the
acoustic background.

### The checks of stage 1 within bins

`precision_by_bin()`, `suggest_thresholds()` and `cell_status()` take a
`by` argument with columns that split each site x species cell. The bins
are joined to the validation tables by the same key (the tables of the
example were drawn with the `"top"` design, so they only illustrate the
call):

```{r}
val_temp <- val_raw |>
  mutate(night = as.character(night)) |>
  left_join(temp_bins, by = c("site", "night"))

precision_by_bin(val_temp, min_n = 15, by = "temp_bin") |>
  filter(site == "BAI", species_folder == "phy_cuv", bin == "[0.9,1]")

suggest_thresholds(val_temp, target_precision = 0.90, min_n = 15,
                   by = "temp_bin") |>
  filter(species_folder == "phy_cuv")
```

A threshold reached in one bin but not in another shows the part of the
gradient where more clips are needed, or where the classifier fails. With
a fitted calibration, `cell_status(fit, validations, by = "temp_bin")`
gives the status of each site x species x bin cell; keep the column in
the validations with `read_validations(keep = "night")` and join the bins.

### Caveats

* **A stratum may be related to the verdict.** Unlike the score, which is
  refused in `strata`, a covariate can be related to whether a detection is
  true: an acoustic index rises when the species calls, and the false
  positive rate may change along the gradient. A calibration that ignores
  the covariate then fits a mixture of bins drawn with unequal inclusion
  probabilities. Include the bin in the calibration (e.g.
  `tp ~ logit_conf + (1 | temp_bin)`, compared with the other candidates
  by `compare_calibration_models()`) or weight the clips by the inverse of
  `inclusion_prob`.
* **The same covariate in the calibration and in the occupancy model.** A
  calibration that varies along the gradient takes over part of what the
  occupancy or detection model would attribute to the covariate, as a
  calibration by month absorbs calling activity. Compare the occupancy
  estimates with and without the covariate in the calibration, and report
  the difference as a sensitivity analysis.
* **Never select by the covariate itself.** Taking the recordings with the
  highest index, as the `"top"` design takes the highest scores, is not a
  probability sample, and its clips cannot calibrate the classifier.
  Stratify, and let the draw within each stratum be random.
* **The covariate must be constant within an occasion** (a night mean for
  nightly or recording occasions, a minute value for minute occasions);
  `select_clips()` refuses strata that vary within an occasion. Occasions
  without a value in `covariates` form a stratum of their own, with a
  warning.
* **More strata, fewer clips per stratum.** Each bin multiplies the number
  of site x species strata; two or three bins per covariate are usually
  enough, and `target_total` or `max_per_species` keep the total effort
  bounded.

A calibration that includes the covariate can be exported to occupancy
models with false positives in two ways. With a random intercept of the
bin, give the bin as a column of `occasion_covariates` and name it in
`calibration_keys` of `export_occupancy_data()`. With the covariate itself
(`tp ~ logit_conf + temp_z`), give it as a column of `occasion_covariates`
on the scale of the model; the export then draws the versions of the
detections itself (schema 1.3; see `vignette("crywolf-integration")`).

The same reasoning applies to the site. The `"random_detections"` design
always draws within site x species, with the same number of occasions per
stratum, so sites with few candidate occasions are reviewed more heavily
than their share of the detections. A global calibration model, without a
site term, then fits a mixture weighted by the design rather than by the
detections; keep the site in the model (the default candidates of
`compare_calibration_models()` with a site intercept) unless the allocation is
proportional to the number of candidate occasions.

## The practical decision

Read the two views together:

* If the effort curve of the chosen model is still rising at the current
  number of clips per cell, review more clips **in every cell**: the pooled
  calibration is limited by the overall effort.
* If the curve has flattened but some cells lack support in stage 1, review
  more clips **only in those cells**, and target the confidence range where
  support is missing. Clips in cells that are already well supported add
  little.
* If a cell is `"exhausted"` (no high-score detections left to review) or
  `"unreliable"` (low precision even at high scores), more validation
  cannot help. Treat the species at that site as
  poorly calibrated, as FrogNet did with the six species left out of the
  community matrices (see `vignette("frognet-workflow")`).

Two caveats apply. First, the curve depends on the formula: a hierarchical
formula needs 'lme4', and its curve can differ markedly from that of the
global model, so draw it for the model that will be used. Second, the curve
depends on how the clips were chosen. The training and test clips of
`calibration_effort()` are drawn from the same reviewed pool, so the AUC
describes discrimination among clips selected by the same design. With the
`"top"` design the pool over-represents high scores; the AUC is conditional
on that design and is not an estimate of the false-positive rate of all
detections. For that, use the `"random_detections"` design, which follows
the observation-confirmation design of
[Chambert et al. (2015)](https://doi.org/10.1890/14-1507.1) (see
`vignette("crywolf-integration")`).

The effort curve can also be drawn inside the whole calibration stage, with
`calibrate(..., effort_curve = TRUE)`; it is then computed for the best
model of the cross-validation and written to `effort_curve.csv`. The
arguments `effort_n` and `effort_reps` set the training sizes and the
number of repetitions.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
sites <- c("ARA", "BAI", "NHE", "XAR")
res <- calibrate(
  validation_files  = val_files,
  prediction_tables = setNames(
    file.path(ex, "birdnet", sites, "BirdNET_SelectionTable.txt"), sites),
  output_dir   = file.path(tempdir(), "calibration"),
  effort_curve = TRUE, effort_n = c(5, 10, 15, 20, 25),
  effort_reps  = 50
)
res$effort
```
